about: THE OUTCOME WEB, version 1 (04 SYSTEM SPECS part 5; research in docs/research/outcome-web-2026-09-28.md). Each link: how a cause measure moves an outcome measure. evidence says how well the link is established (researched, provisional, contested, about-zero, to-confirm). size is the proportional change in the outcome per unit of the cause (see per); null means the size is set when both measures exist in the world. about-zero links are zero on purpose and tested. Sources are for developers only and never appear on a player screen. A cause named law:<qualified question key> is what the law in force says on a policy question (governing/law-in-force.ts): 1 when it says yes, 0 when it says no, and unrecorded where no law has answered it. A law cause is measured from the place's law on the calibration date (calibratedAt): its base data already includes the law in force then, so only a change from it moves the outcome. law:us-federal-positions:<key> is a question only Congress answers. A link's size is a baseline, not a literal number: each world draws the size for each place from the link's range (the spread the research reports), or from a default spread by evidence (researched 25% either way, provisional 50%, contested from none to twice the size). About-zero links stay at zero.

links.per: adoption of statutory public-place stand-your-ground law versus no such adoption in the controlled pooled study
links.anchor: Increases firearm homicides (RAND: supportive)
links.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8861849/
why: The study associates statutory stand-your-ground adoption with higher monthly firearm-homicide rates after controlling for comparison states, seasonality and long-term trends.
Its treatment is an extension of legal immunity for lethal self-defense outside the home to places where a person has a legal right to be.

That legal change can alter the perceived legal consequences of choosing lethal force. The authors describe possible encouragement of otherwise avoidable deadly encounters; deterrence is the competing explanation.

A person chooses whether to use lethal force in a particular encounter from the situation and their own record. A firearm discharge can physically kill another person. The aggregate estimate does not choose that action or victim.
Legal rule: statutory protection for qualifying public-place self-defense; physical fact: lethal force can kill. Actual behavioral mediation is not identified by this study.

conditions.strongerWeakerAbsent: Large increases in total/firearm homicide associations cluster in several Southern states; reported combined outcome increases16.2%–33.5%. Some states have no statistically significant associations. That combined range is not a firearm-only numerical interval.
conditions.rangeMeaning: [0.03,0.13] is the published95%interval around the pooled firearm-homicide rate ratio minus1. It is not a distribution of local effects, not a bound on every state, and not a territory transport estimate.

links.per: percentage point of residents receiving SNAP that a law or other cause moved
links.anchor: SNAP cuts a household's chance of food insecurity about 30%. 51.1% of households that received SNAP in 2024 were food insecure, so without it about 73% would be: 21.9 points more for each household that loses SNAP. SNAP households average 1.9 people and all households 2.5, so a point of residents is 1.3% of households, and food insecurity rises 0.29 points, 2.1% of the 13.7% national rate. The low end reads the 30% against the rate with SNAP (15.3 points); the high end is a quarter above the center. Only the part of SNAP receipt that a law or other cause moved counts: the share's own drift stands for changes in need, which move food insecurity the other way.
links.source: Ratcliffe, McKernan and Zhang 2011, American Journal of Agricultural Economics 93(4); USDA ERS, Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 (ERR-358), table 8; USDA FNS, Characteristics of SNAP Households: Fiscal Year 2023; Census Bureau, America's Families and Living Arrangements: 2024

links.anchor: Behavior effects differ by program. Perry Preschool cut violent-crime arrests by age 40 by a third (32% vs. 48%), and Chicago's Child-Parent Centers cut violent juvenile arrests 41% (9.0% vs. 15.3%), both for low-income children. Tennessee's program left sixth graders with more discipline problems (0.09 standard deviations more offenses). People under 18 made about 9.8% of violent-crime arrests in 2019. absentWhen: The first enrolled cohort has not reached its teens, or no child enrolled.
